items.text: multiple locations across Hamilton County, Indiana (Fishers, Noblesville, Carmel)
Operating continuously since 2014 — over 11 years, thousands of athletes trained.

Governing voice archetype: the Vulnerable Mentor. Warm, direct, scientifically grounded. Does not lead with credentials or superiority — leads with shared experience, naming the specific moments parents have already lived and never said out loud: "The sideline. The post-game silence in the car. The 'needs to work on speed' note from a coach. The kid who tries harder than everyone else and is still not the fastest one on the field."
Dedicated full-time to youth athletic development. Coaches and staff who attend athletes' games 40 minutes away because results matter beyond the training floor.
NSCA Certified Strength and Conditioning Specialist (CSCS): "The gold standard in the industry. The same certification required of D1 university and NFL strength coaches."
Trained 7× Pro Bowl, 6× All-Pro NFL offensive lineman Zack Martin (Dallas Cowboys)
Trained Super Bowl champion Ted Karras
Featured in Inside Indiana Business and Towne Post Network
60+ Google Reviews, 4.9+ average rating across locations

"Most youth 'speed trainers' have a weekend certification and a whistle. Coach Graham Wilkerson holds the NSCA's Certified Strength and Conditioning Specialist credential — the gold standard in the industry. The same certification required of D1 strength coaches and NFL performance staffs. He holds a Master's degree in Athletic Coaching Education. He's trained 7× Pro Bowl, 6× All-Pro NFL lineman Zack Martin. Super Bowl champion Ted Karras. NFL starter Nick Martin."

Graham's unique perspective comes from the gap he observed between professional-level VBT precision and youth-level training chaos. Having applied velocity-based training at the NFL level — where every bar speed is tracked to the hundredth of a meter per second — he then watched youth athletes finish conditioning sessions visibly slowing through tired reps while coaches counted them as productive work. His perspective is not that youth coaches are bad. His perspective is that youth coaches are operating without the technology that makes the difference between productive and anti-productive reps visible.

"I was working with an NFL athlete and tracking bar velocity to the hundredth of a meter per second on every rep. Then I watched a group of 10-year-olds finish a conditioning session running their slowest laps. And I thought: they're programming themselves to be slower. And no one knows it."
items.notes: From Discovery Narrative, to be confirmed with Graham

items.text: "Everything I used at the professional level works here. It works BETTER here. Because the nervous system at age 9 is doing something it will never do again — it's forming the foundational movement patterns for the next 20 years of athletic life."

"After training NFL All-Pro Zack Martin, Super Bowl champion Ted Karras, and NFL starter Nick Martin, I identified a pattern: the same velocity-based principles that kept these athletes at the top of their game could be adapted for developing athletes — if you applied them during the critical developmental window. That insight became The Velocity Code™."

The early warning signs are the first quiet moments of divergence — the child at the bottom of a sprint drill, the first season of not starting, the coach's note that says "needs to work on speed" without any prescription for what to actually do. At this stage the parent has not yet sounded the alarm. They're still operating on hope.

"My son, who is 10 years old, isn't particularly athletic. He tends to be a bit clumsy and awkward. As his peers become more skilled and competitive, I'm noticing that he's losing interest in these activities." — r/daddit

"Although he may not be the most athletic player, he demonstrates a strong work ethic and intelligence on the field... It's important to communicate that the reason he's not getting as much playing time is because his peers are currently stronger and quicker." — r/CoachingYouthSports

"In my experience coaching children aged 8 to 12, I've noticed that the standout player at age 9 often doesn't maintain that status through high school. At that younger age, travel teams tend to favor those who are the largest and fastest." — r/CoachingYouthSports

The parent has now invested — travel teams, private coaches, speed camps. The money is real. The effort is real. The child is working. And the gap is widening, not closing. The programs have been tried and have delivered nothing measurable. The parent begins to suspect something is wrong with the industry itself but doesn't have a framework to explain it.

"I just didn't realize back then that the new normal is that club sports are pretty much necessary to have a chance to be a big part of a high school team... I question my decision to not have them do travel teams when I go to games and watch them not start the game, or maybe not get in at all." — r/indianapolis

"Many of these players, just 9 years old, are already working with private pitching coaches. It makes me feel disheartened for my son, who is just a casual participant, as I worry he might never reach a level where he can compete in high school baseball." — r/indianapolis
"I overheard a coach telling a parent that if their 8-year-old didn't already have a hitting coach, they wouldn't stand a chance in competition." — r/indianapolis
"This coincided with the fact that other children who had begun training earlier were reaching their full potential while he was still catching up." — r/Homeplate

"There's no middle ground. Either you are all in and get private training just to be able to keep up with the for-profit enterprises that are running these leagues or you fall back into rec with a mix of kids that don't really want to be there." — r/indianapolis

The crisis is not primarily athletic — it is the moment the parent watches the child's confidence collapse in real time. The child who says "I'm scared I'll mess up." The child threatening to quit if moved down. The parent going home and doing math on everything they've spent.
"months of sitting out severely impacted his confidence. He became the player that other parents wanted to see replaced." — r/youthsoccer
"I'm worried he might be moved back down, and he's mentioned that he would quit if that happens. That's a heavy burden for a 10-year-old to bear." — r/youthsoccer

"This weekend we were out practicing before his games on Sunday and I was very sad for him because he said 'I'm not as good as the rest of my team and I'm scared I'll mess up'. Makes me so sad that he has those feelings at such a young age and already feels this pressure." — r/indianapolis
"I see a reality: Slow as f*ck literally means just that. Out of all track members on the team, I think he is top 2. Top 2 dead last." — r/mildlyinfuriating
"I have a deep love for my son and I'm committed to helping him succeed, even if he appears to be moving in slow motion on the field." — r/mildlyinfuriating

The nadir is the parent doing the arithmetic — the literal math of what has been spent versus what has been produced — and arriving at a number that doesn't make sense. The grief is real. The guilt is internalized. The parent oscillates between blaming the child (the effort explanation), blaming themselves (the "I haven't done enough" explanation), and blaming the industry (the "it's all a money grab" explanation). None of these have solutions. They are waiting for the explanation that redirects blame to the method — the one variable that is actually changeable.
"I found myself navigating through the stages of grief." — r/youthsoccer

"I won't shy away from admitting that I've lost some sleep over it. As parents, we all desire the best for our children, and it can be challenging to come to terms with another adult's evaluations of them." — r/youthsoccer

"Our primary concern is, of course, our daughter and how this situation might impact her confidence. We want to avoid telling her that she's currently at the lower end of the roster so she doesn't get even more nervous or less confidence." — r/youthsoccer

"Initially, I viewed this as a lack of effort on his part. However, upon reflection, I realized that I may have inadvertently limited his opportunities and potential as a parent. I recognized my own lack of drive to help him reach his fullest potential, and I take responsibility for that." — r/Homeplate
"I believe he gained more from that $2000 [speed/agility program] than the over $10,000 we spent sending him to club ball." — r/lacrosse
"My hesitation has always been about weighing the financial investment against the effort put forth." — r/Homeplate
"I've been questioning whether the expense is justified." — r/youthsoccer
